  "text": "The laundrette on Bell Street had one machine nobody used.

Its door was padlocked. A handwritten notice said: PERSONAL ITEMS ONLY.

When my wedding ring disappeared, the attendant handed me a token.

“Machine seven,” she said.

“I haven’t got anything to wash.”

“Check your pockets.”

Inside my coat was a receipt from the restaurant where Daniel had proposed. I hadn’t seen it in twelve years.

The attendant unlocked the machine.

“Cold cycle. Don’t watch the drum.”

I put the receipt inside.

For twenty minutes, I studied a poster about removing bloodstains. Behind me, something heavy knocked against the glass.

When the machine stopped, my ring lay on the rubber seal.

The receipt was gone.

At home, Daniel asked where I’d been.

“The laundrette.”

He looked at my hand.

“That’s pretty. Where did you get it?”

I laughed until I realised he was serious.

Our wedding photographs now showed us standing several feet apart. In one, I was holding somebody else’s bouquet.

I went back before closing.

The attendant listened without surprise.

“Found things need somewhere to have been lost from.”

“Put it back.”

She gave me another token.

This time, my pocket held a folded hospital blanket. A small name was stitched into its corner.

We had never had children.

From inside machine seven came a single, impatient kick.

“Can I choose something else?” I whispered.

The attendant glanced towards the other machines.

Every drum had stopped turning. Behind each round window, wet clothes sagged into the shape of someone sitting down.

“Not now,” she said.

At home, my phone began to ring.

The screen said Mummy."
